definition.text: Harness is the agent runtime: the process that actually carries out one agent's work, driven through a session over the Agent Client Protocol. This repo's own substrate table names the adapter directly -- "goose `v1.46.0`" -- reached over "Agent Client Protocol | goose" -- and records the isolation unit it runs inside as "One microVM per agent", one harness process per cell. Independent of this repo, goose's own documentation describes it more broadly as "goose is a general-purpose AI agent that runs on your machine.", not a coding-only tool.

One microVM per agent
goose is a general-purpose AI agent that runs on your machine.

standards.role: governs the wire contract the harness speaks to whatever opens its session and drives it -- a standard protocol between editors and coding agents modelled explicitly on LSP: "ACP fixes this with a simple idea borrowed from LSP: define a standard wire protocol between editors and agents, so any agent can plug into any editor." This repo's own substrate row names the same transport: "Agent Client Protocol (ACP), JSON-RPC over stdio".
standards.covers: does not govern which model backs the agent, its internal tool loop, or its own reasoning process -- those stay adapter detail behind the turn, and the protocol's local binding is a subprocess, not a network service: for a local agent, the editor "spawns the agent as a subprocess", per this repo's own substrate row naming the same JSON-RPC-over-stdio transport for its adapter.

landscape.text: Reading the evidence below, the differentiator among ACP-speaking harnesses looks less like features and more like role and governance (this repo's own reading, not a source's claim). ACP itself moved from a single-editor mechanism to a shared layer quickly: "Zed introduced ACP in August 2025, and JetBrains joined shortly after." -- and it is explicitly modelled on a prior standardization: "Think LSP, but for AI agents instead of language servers." Within that shared protocol, goose is not simply a passive runtime a client opens a session against: goose's own documentation states "goose works as an ACP server — connect from Zed, JetBrains, or VS Code — and can use ACP agents like Claude Code and Codex as providers", i.e. it can also act as the client driving other harnesses. On governance, this corpus's other citable mentions of Goose alongside other agents -- a page listing broad Agent Skills adoption ("Adoption is far wider than most security teams realize - 40+ clients including Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, VS Code, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, Goose, and data platforms like Databricks and Snowflake.") and danilchenko.dev's ACP agent registry cited above -- name no steward at all. goose's own site, fetched 2026-09-10, is the only sourced statement of who currently stewards it: "goose is part of the Agentic AI Foundation at the Linux Foundation — ensuring the project remains vendor-neutral, community-governed, and open for the long term." This corpus has no citable record naming who stewarded goose before that (see gaps). On the specific "smallest footprint" framing this repo's own reference model gives the card: the only footprint-adjacent trait found is that goose is "Built in Rust for performance and portability." rather than a scripted process -- a real implementation trait, but not itself a comparative measurement against Claude Code, Cursor, or any other ACP-speaking agent, none of which this corpus has evidence on.

usage.text: A caller does not address the harness directly; it is reached only through the one observable per-turn primitive this repo has measured on it: cancellation. This repo's own substrate table records "session/cancel mid-tool-call ends the turn in ~8s against a 45s operation, zero trailing frames" -- a request to end the turn is accepted, not a kill, and the caller keeps taking frames until a terminal one arrives carrying the stop reason.

gaps.what: This repo has no harness/ directory dedicated to the agent-runtime capability. The harness/containment harness (built for isolation, card 3.3) is reused to prove the runtime's own cancellation contract, and its live path -- the one that actually launches goose over ACP inside a Firecracker cell -- has never been run: adapters/live.py exists, but the harness's own provenance record states it "has never been executed against firecracker-cell@.service or goose, so the systemd start and stop commands, the jail path, the broker counter file, the ACP transport choice and the stop-reason mapping are unverified there."
gaps.why_it_matters: A card marked built whose only evidence for the live runtime is code that has never run against a real goose process is a claim about the adapter existing, not about it working; the distinction the repo itself draws between measured and claimed.
gaps.research_query: has harness/containment's live adapter ever been executed against a real goose process and a real Firecracker cell, and with what recorded output

gaps.what: The card's own tagline for this element ("goose - smallest footprint, one per cell") is not backed by any comparative measurement in this corpus. The only footprint-relevant fact found is that goose is a compiled Rust binary rather than a scripted process, which is a real trait but not a measured comparison against Claude Code, Cursor, or any other named swap candidate.
gaps.why_it_matters: A superlative ("smallest") asserted without a comparison point is exactly the kind of unevidenced claim this card exists to catch; it should either be sourced to a real benchmark or restated as a design choice this repo has not measured.
gaps.research_query: binary size, memory footprint, or cold-start comparison across goose, Claude Code, Cursor and other ACP-speaking agent harnesses

gaps.what: goose's CURRENT governance is well-evidenced (goose's own site, fetched 2026-09-10: "goose is part of the Agentic AI Foundation at the Linux Foundation — ensuring the project remains vendor-neutral, community-governed, and open for the long term."), but this repo's corpus has no citable record naming who stewarded or owned goose before that. An earlier version of this card cited a record for the label "Block's Goose"; on repair, that record's own page (a broad Agent Skills adoption list) was found to name Goose plainly, with no possessive and no steward named at all, so the 'Block' attribution has been dropped as unsourced rather than replaced.
gaps.why_it_matters: cap-provenance and cap-identity both care who actually stands behind a component this repo depends on. This corpus can now state goose's current steward with a real citation, but a reader asking 'who ran it before AAIF' would find nothing sourced here -- that gap should stay open rather than being filled by an unsourced assumption.
gaps.research_query: is there a citable, publisher-authored source (not a search-engine snippet) for who stewarded or owned goose before it moved to the Agentic AI Foundation, and when that move happened

gaps.what: This card was assigned standard badge 'none' in docs/reference/reference-model.json, yet this repo's own Part B substrate table names a standard for this exact capability: the row reads "Agent runtime | Agent Client Protocol | goose | ..." (F-b3-05). The badge and this repo's own fact record disagree about whether Agent runtime has a named standard. The same pattern holds for the two sibling cards in this area (3.2 Model Interface, 3.3 Runtime/Sandbox), both also badged 'none' while their own Part B rows name a standard, so this looks like a systematic gap in how docs/reference/reference-model.json's badge field was populated rather than something specific to this card.
gaps.why_it_matters: A reader who trusts the badge alone would conclude this element has no governing standard, when this repo's own substrate table says otherwise; the reference model's summary view and its own source-of-truth table are out of sync.
gaps.research_query: was the reference-model.json standard badge field deliberately left null for Core Agent cards, or is it an oversight in how PASS.md's Part B table was transcribed into the reference model
